transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-06
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 43 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Jordan (Redwood CSM - joined 10m), Dr. Aisha Rahman, Ethan Morales, Priya Singh, Luca Moretti (security)

Summary: Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics — streaming, key parameters (temperature/top_p/max_tokens), and resilient retry/backoff patterns. Heavy focus on perf and security: questions about latency SLO, SOC2, VPC options and encryption/KMS. Agreed next steps: send SOC2 docs, share benchmark script, schedule 2-week POC kickoff.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account. Quick round robin?
[00:05] Aisha: Hi I'm Aisha, lead AI at Crescent HealthTech. We're trying to evaluate hosted inference for clinical summarization features.
[00:10] Ethan: Ethan, backend, I'll be running benchmarks and integration.
[00:12] Priya: Priya, product — making sure timelines and success criteria align.
[00:15] Luca: Luca, security. I'll chime in on compliance and key management.
[00:20] Liam: Liam here, SE — I'll walk through the API demo and show streaming + retry patterns.
[00:24] Maya: Goal for today is short hosted-gen demo, show streaming behavior, parameter impacts and a recommended retry/backoff strategy for low-latency apps. Leave time at the end for security Qs. Sound good?
[00:31] Aisha: Sounds good. Our big needs: sub-200ms token latencies for short prompts if possible, and tight control over PII — must not persist PHI in logs.
[00:40] Liam: Great, noted. Redwood hosted has opt-in data retention and encryption at rest. We'll show console bits where you can toggle retention and connect to KMS. There are also private/dedicated options if you need network isolation.

--- Demo start ---
[02:05] Liam: Alright I'll share my screen, walking the basic chat generation endpoint. First we call /v1/chat/completions with a streaming flag. The stream sends events for partial tokens, similar to SSE.
[02:25] (screen share noise)
[02:31] Liam: Here's a simple prompt: "Summarize this clinical note in three bullets". On the response side you get an event per chunk, and the client can render progressively. You can control chunk size with the stream_chunk_size param but generally the runtime optimizes for latency.
[03:00] Ethan: Is chunk size client side or server side? We worry about lots of small events increasing overhead.
[03:06] Liam: Mostly server-side; the engine emits tokens as they are generated. For low-overhead you can use the streaming buffer parameter or request a minimum chunk byte-size — we recommend batching small tokens for mobile clients. In the console Optimize tab we also suggest batching heuristics based on your traffic profile.
[03:28] Priya: What's the default timeout for a streaming response? Do we need a separate heartbeat?
[03:34] Liam: Default idle timeout is 60s for a stream. For robustness we recommend client-side idempotency keys on the creation request, and an exponential backoff + jitter on reconnection.
[03:42] Maya: Quick note on idempotency: Redwood API supports idempotency_key header for creation calls so retries don't double-charge or double-run the model.

[04:10] Liam: Moving on to params — temperature, top_p, max_new_tokens. For clinical summarization we usually suggest temperature between 0.0 and 0.3 to keep outputs deterministic. top_p can be left default, but if you need strict determinism set top_p to 0. 
[04:35] Aisha: Makes sense, we need stable outputs for downstream heuristics. Any notes on tokenization differences across model variants?
[04:43] Liam: Good question. Tokenization can affect token accounting and latency. Redwood catalog lists per-model tokenization and we surface estimated token counts in the console. Also watch out for long prefix context — KV cache affects memory and latency.
[05:00] Ethan: You mentioned KV cash earlier in doc, did you mean K-V cache?
[05:04] Liam: Yes, sorry, K-V cache — sometimes speech-to-text autosubst. The transcript engine munges that.

[05:20] (short cough in background)
[05:25] Liam: Now demoing a retry sequence. Scenario: intermittent 5xxs from runtime under burst. Recommended pattern: immediate small retry for transient errors up to 2 times, then exponential backoff (200ms, 600ms, 1800ms) plus jitter. If using streaming, prefer reconnect with same idempotency key and fetch last acknowledged token index if you track that on client.
[06:00] Priya: If we reconnect mid-stream, do we get duplicate tokens?
[06:03] Liam: We try to make retries idempotent, but depending on model variant you might get partial overlap. Best practice: buffer client-side and dedupe by sequence number returned in stream events. Redwood stream emits sequence_id metadata in each event (console docs show examples).
[06:22] Luca: Sequence IDs are useful — is that metadata encrypted?
[06:25] Liam: Metadata in transit is TLS; at rest it's encrypted — but we can toggle retention off for sensitive workloads.

[07:00] Maya: Quick qualification: what's your average prompt length and target QPS?
[07:05] Ethan: Currently small — avg 80 tokens request, 40 tokens expected response. Peak QPS around 120, concurrency up to 30 during spike windows.
[07:16] Liam: Okay that maps well to hosted. If you need lower jitter during peaks we recommend Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools). For hosted we can set burst policy and soft-limits.
[07:30] Aisha: For cost estimation, can you show the token pricing model?
[07:35] Maya: We'll send a tailored cost sheet, but generally hosted per-token pricing scales with model family and throughput. In console Optimize we surface per-route token breakdowns and suggest quantized model variants for cost/cpu tradeoffs.

[08:15] Liam: Back to streaming behavior — here's a live example with an intentionally long response. Notice the stream yields partial sentences, and the client can flush to UI progressively. If a socket error occurs we reconnect and resume where possible.
[09:05] (network hiccup sound)
[09:12] Liam: That was simulated; you saw a reconnect and the client re-requested with idempotency key. The server returned an 'already processed' acknowledgement and served the rest of the tokens.

[10:00] Priya: Are there SDKs that handle reconnection/backoff for us?
[10:03] Liam: Yes, Redwood SDKs for Node and Python include a streaming helper that handles partial event parsing, idempotency, reconnects with jittered backoff, and exposes per-token events with sequence ids. It's open-source on our GitHub and we maintain examples in the Console snippets.

[11:00] Luca: On encryption — KMS options? We need customer-managed keys.
[11:06] Maya: We support AWS KMS and customer-supplied keys for Dedicated/Private deployments. For hosted we offer a managed KMS but can enable bring-your-own-key for enterprise. I'll attach our KMS integration notes.
[11:25] Luca: And audit logs? We need immutable request logs for 90 days for compliance.
[11:30] Liam: Audit logs are available as an add-on. They include request traces, model version, token counts, and errors. You can stream logs to your S3 or SIEM. Retention period configurable.

[12:10] Ethan: Quick perf question — how do you get sub-200ms token time? We use small prompt/response pairs. Any guidance?
[12:16] Liam: Latency depends on model size and sequence length. To optimize: pin a low-latency model, use prefix caching for repeated context, enable continuous batching settings in the console to reduce cold-token latency, and use smaller max_new_tokens. For highest determinism, use quantized model variants but be aware of small quality differences.

[13:05] Aisha: About data residency — we have EU clinical data. Can you pin hosted to eu-west regions?
[13:10] Maya: Yes, hosted supports region-specific endpoints. We can pin traffic to EU regions and restrict storage per region. For strict residency you can choose Private with a VPC or Dedicated with region placement.

[14:00] Liam: Quick note: model rollouts and fallbacks — Redwood can route requests by policy. Example: route to cheaper quantized variant for non-critical requests, and fallback to full precision when quality metrics degrade. We also support automatic fallback during capacity constraints.
[14:25] Priya: Who sets the routing policy? Is that configurable in the Console?
[14:29] Liam: Yes, routing policies live in the Console under Deployments > Routing. You can define predicates (latency threshold, cost budget, region) and fallbacks. We have presets for latency-sensitive apps.

[15:00] (Jordan joins)
[15:12] Jordan: Hey all, I popped in to align on the POC scope — quick question on usage caps for trial accounts.
[15:18] Maya: For pilots we typically grant sandbox credits and set hard caps. Jordan will coordinate the initial quota and a billing contact.

[16:00] Aisha: Security follow-up: do you do customer-managed audit reviews? Can we run a pentest?
[16:06] Luca: (overlap) We typically need attestation.
[16:08] Maya: We do annual third-party pentesting and provide SOC2 Type II reports. For customers needing pentest on our integration layer, we have a process — need to sign the NDA and scope doc. I'll send the process doc.

[17:00] Liam: Back to resiliency — let's outline a recommended client-side retry recipe: 1) Use idempotency on create calls. 2) For 429 or 5xx: immediate 100-200ms retry up to 2 times. 3) Then exponential backoff with full jitter (600ms, 1500ms, 3s) and cap at 10s. 4) For streaming: reconnect and request from last sequence_id, dedupe tokens. 5) Add observable hooks for token lags and error rates to trigger routing to Dedicated.
[18:00] Ethan: What about cost on retries? If a retry partially executed and resumed will we be billed extra?
[18:05] Maya: Billing is tied to model compute. If retry is a re-creation that runs model again, you may be charged but idempotency and request acknowledgement reduce double-work. For streaming reconnects that just resume, billing is for the token generation itself — we'll share exact billing semantics for edge cases in the doc.

[19:00] Priya: For our acceptance criteria for POC: latency targets (95th <250ms), accuracy threshold on summary ROUGE-like metric, and zero retention for PHI. Can you support these?
[19:10] Liam: Yes, we can aim for that. The POC will include a benchmark harness to measure p95 latency and quality. We'll instrument it in the Console with traces.

[20:00] (Liam runs a short console tour)
[21:10] Liam: Console Optimize will show per-route cost, latency distribution, and suggestions: batching increase, alternative model suggestions, quantization profile. You can export suggestions as a one-click apply.
[21:50] Aisha: Could Optimize automatically suggest a fallback when latency spikes?
[21:55] Liam: We can configure automated rollback or fallback policies triggered by latency SLO breaches. Those are safety-first configs — we usually test them in staging.

[23:00] Luca: Any encryption at transit beyond TLS? We need proof of TLS configuration and cipher suites for our security team.
[23:06] Maya: We'll attach our TLS configuration and cert rotation notes. We also support mTLS in Dedicated/private setups.

[24:00] Ethan: For the benchmark script you mentioned — will it emulate streaming behavior?
[24:04] Liam: Yes, our benchmark harness can emulate concurrent streaming clients, measure per-token latency and p95/p99, and produce a CSV you can ingest. I'll send the script and a small sample dataset.

[25:00] (small background chatter)
[26:10] Priya: Timeline-wise, if we kickoff POC week of Apr 20, how long to stand up sandbox and get initial results?
[26:16] Maya: We can provision sandbox credentials within 48 hours once we have the stakeholder list. Initial bench results in 3-5 business days.

[27:00] Aisha: One more thing — we need to limit model hallucination for clinical notes. Any guardrails?
[27:06] Liam: Provide a hallucination-reduction recipe: low temperature, strict max_tokens, use retrieval augmentation with pinned source snippets, and apply post-generation filters. We also offer a reranker endpoint to score responses before returning to users.

[28:00] Ethan: Reranker — is that an extra cost?
[28:04] Maya: It's billed like any other model call; it's often cheaper because rerankers are smaller models. Optimize suggests when to rerank based on your quality metrics.

[30:00] (quick recap)
[30:10] Maya: Recap: Showed streaming, params for determinism, recommended client retry/backoff recipe, discussed encryption/KMS, audit logs, residency. Next steps we already listed — May send SOC2, bench script, schedule POC for Apr 20 week.

[31:00] Aisha: That sounds good. Could you also include a short sample integration in our stack (we use Go + Kube)?
[31:06] Liam: Yes, we have Go examples and Kubernetes sidecar patterns for streaming. I'll include a small Go example that uses the Node-like streaming helper behavior and an ingress pattern to keep connections sticky.

[32:00] Priya: Any gotchas for mobile clients?
[32:03] Liam: For mobile, prefer aggregate partials to avoid battery and spiky network usage; use smaller streaming frames and server-side buffering. Consider using a gateway to normalize streams for mobile.

[33:00] Luca: Onboarding docs and security checklist — can we get a checklist for infra to review?
[33:05] Maya: Yes, full security checklist and onboarding runbook coming in the follow-up packet.

[34:00] (Jordan: confirming sandbox credit process)
[34:10] Jordan: We'll allocate $X of sandbox credits for the POC and a sandbox project with RBAC.

[35:00] Aisha: Anything else we should know before POC?
[35:04] Liam: Think about your failure modes — how should the app degrade on model unavailability: cached short summaries, user notifications, or fallback to smaller local model. We'll help define a graceful degradation plan during the POC.

[36:00] Priya: Okay good. We'll prepare the traffic profile and stakeholder list.
[36:05] Ethan: I'll produce the traffic profile and a sample dataset with redaction markers.

[37:00] Maya: Great, so action items captured. We'll follow up with the packet and the benchmark harness.

[38:00] (closing)
[38:05] Aisha: Thanks, that was really helpful.
[38:08] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[38:10] Luca: Appreciate the compliance answers.
[38:12] Maya: Thanks all — we'll send the materials and book the POC kickoff. Expect an email tomorrow with links.
[38:20] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcript had a few mis-hearings (K-V cache -> KV cash, some overlap on names) — cleaned minimally.
